name: Nige
title: RT by @nigescore: Astra Ultra did not cook sports-grade vision AI. Gave it a 30s football clip from our subnet private track. Frame-level events, JSON, annotated video. Ground truth and the published scoring rules only after it committed. 22 predictions. 17 real events. 15 inside the action windows. 7 extras. 2 misses. Precision 68.18%. Recall 88.24%. F1 76.92%. Our Bittensor eval, SN44: 0%. Matches after timing decay: 16.538 False positives: −20.300 GT weight: 25.600 score = max(0, (16.538 − 20.300) / 25.600) = 0 Three extra take-ons and two extra tackles were 14.6 penalty points. It also misread the late interception/clearance. Rare actions pay more when you hit them and tax you harder when you invent them. Perfect timestamps on the matches still would not have cleared that bill. This was one offline replay of the published scorer. Unchanged preds. Not live latency. Not a season. The point is simpler than the arithmetic. F1 is what you post. SN44 is what you get paid on. Real matches, messy cameras, hard negatives, and a 30-second clock are not the same sport as a nice 15s clip to aura farm on Twitter.

title: Subnet 44 @webuildscore is expanding. We’re incentivising training for a new vision-language model: Satori. Satori reasons AND grounds. It doesn’t just answer questions about an image. It points to the evidence. - Reason about scenes - Detect and segment objects - Read text - Count entities - Ground claims in pixels Most VLMs are split: strong reasoning OR strong grounding. Detection models localise, but can’t talk. Chatty VLMs describe fluently, but can’t prove it. Satori sits at the intersection. We’re starting with a 7B base model.

name: Templar
title: Crucible, Templar's pre-training platform, has completed its first production end-to-end training runs. The latest trained an 8B model on 50.53B tokens across 48 distributed A100s, at an estimated $0.1202 per million tokens of GPU rental. The run reached 48.3% effective MFU. At AWS p4de Capacity Blocks pricing, a 48-A100 cluster operating at the literature-derived 65% compute ceiling comes to an estimated $0.1686 per million tokens. Crucible's measured $0.1202 was about 29% lower after its low-bandwidth overhead. The comparison excludes R2 storage and operations. The full writeup shows the method and accounting. Blog: https://www.tplr.ai/publications/blog/introducing-crucible
